proposals.name: Ratwretches
proposals.entry:
"Don't corner one. Don't feed one. And don't ever let one decide your cellar is warmer than his."

Ratwretches are a despised race of long-limbed, rat-faced people found in Fogport's oldest cellars, collapsed districts, drainage works, abandoned factories, canal tunnels and the immense neglected spaces beneath the city.

They are generally taller than humans when standing straight, although few do. Their bodies are narrow through the shoulders and enormously flexible. Their coats range from rust-red and brown to soot-black, piebald and sickly gray. Their tails are naked, scarred and surprisingly expressive.

Most Fogporters consider them vermin. Ratwretches know this perfectly well. They aren't especially fond of Fogporters either.

Nobody Knows Where They Came From

There are no reliable records of Ratwretches before the Catastrophe.

The Civic Order claims they are ordinary rats enlarged and altered by Catastrophic magic. This theory has one enormous political advantage: you don't have to give a rat civil rights.

Some physicians insist Ratwretches are clearly humanoid and therefore probably descend from people transformed during the Catastrophe.

A more disturbing theory concerns the Old Hunger Winter. Thousands of survivors sheltered beneath Fogport after the Catastrophe. Several underground refugee camps eventually stopped answering census workers. Officials assumed they had died.

Ratwretches become extremely hostile when anyone suggests this connection.

Their own explanation is simpler. They say: "We came from our mothers." Further questions are generally unsuccessful.

The Unwelcome People

Ratwretches occupy an uncomfortable place between citizen and pest. They can be arrested, fined, taxed and sentenced to hard labor. But many landlords won't rent to them, businesses refuse them service, employers pay them less, and respectable neighborhoods periodically demand their removal.

Signs reading NO DOGS — NO RATWRETCHES — NO CREDIT are common.

The Civic Order occasionally conducts Rat Abatement Campaigns. Whether Ratwretches are included depends largely upon which official you ask. And whether there are witnesses.

The Great Ratwretch Obsession: Fit

Ratwretches are fascinated by spaces. Not maps. Not architecture. Spaces.

They possess an almost instinctive understanding of whether something—or someone—can fit through an opening. A Ratwretch will glance at a ventilation grate and immediately know: Head fits. Shoulder doesn't. Remove left hinge.

They measure constantly: doorways, pipes, chimneys, cracks, drains, floorboards, cargo crates, window frames and human skulls.

Their preferred unit of measurement is their own body. A Ratwretch might describe a passage as "One shoulder, sideways, breath out." Or: "Child easy. You difficult. Big man impossible."

They have no difficulty understanding conventional measurements. They simply consider them unnecessarily theoretical.

Ratwretch Architecture

Ratwretches do not construct underground kingdoms. They colonize unused volume: the cavity behind a retaining wall, the gap beneath a raised floor, a forgotten ventilation shaft, the hollow center of a bridge pier, or the space between an old sewer and the newer sewer constructed directly above it.

A Ratwretch settlement may contain thirty people within yards of a busy street. Entrances are deliberately uncomfortable. A human entering a Ratwretch home should expect to crawl. Then squeeze. Then turn sideways. Then climb. Then discover an unexpectedly large room containing twenty Ratwretches staring at him.

Their homes are surprisingly comfortable. Ratwretches adore warmth. Little iron stoves burn constantly. Kettles simmer. Bedding is piled ridiculously deep. Walls are covered with rugs and scraps of fabric to keep out drafts.

They are also obsessive about doors. A prosperous Ratwretch home may have twelve entrances. A very prosperous one has twenty. A Ratwretch with only one way out considers himself practically imprisoned.

Borrowing

Ratwretches have a flexible understanding of ownership. They understand perfectly well that your shovel belongs to you. They simply don't understand why that should prevent them using it while you aren't.

This is called borrowing.

Ratwretches borrow tools, food, coal, laundry, boots, furniture and occasionally livestock. They are genuinely offended by accusations of theft if they intended to return the item.

The problem is that eventually has an unusually broad meaning in Ratwretch culture. A Ratwretch may return a stolen saucepan three years later and expect the matter to be settled. It may even have been repaired.

Knives

Nearly every adult Ratwretch carries a knife. Usually a terrible one: rusty kitchen knives, broken butcher blades, sharpened files, snapped bayonets and pieces of sawblade wrapped in cloth.

They use them constantly: cutting rope, opening crates, scraping rust, digging mortar, cleaning fish, removing nails and cutting new holes through walls.

Ratwretches find the human distinction between tool and weapon rather silly. A knife cuts things. Sometimes the thing is cheese. Sometimes the thing is you.

Their Teeth Never Stop

Ratwretch incisors grow throughout their lives. Consequently they must gnaw constantly. Most carry a chew—a piece of hardwood, bone, horn, leather, soft brick or scrap metal specifically intended for wearing down the teeth.

A Ratwretch thinking deeply will often chew while staring at you. Humans find this extremely unsettling. Especially during negotiations.

Different materials have social associations. Children chew wood. Laborers often chew leather or bone. Old Ratwretches favor soft brass. A Ratwretch chewing iron is either showing off or extremely angry.

The Clicking

Ratwretches communicate normally enough, although their voices tend toward rasping consonants. But around humans they frequently make another sound: click-click-click.

Humans assumed for centuries that this was meaningless animal noise. It isn't.

Ratwretches use tooth-clicks, tongue pops, tail movements and tiny changes in posture as a parallel layer of conversation. Two Ratwretches may politely negotiate with a shopkeeper while simultaneously conducting an entirely different conversation about him.

Nobody has successfully produced a complete Ratwretch click dictionary. The Ratwretches think this is hilarious.

Names

Ratwretch names are usually short and abrasive: Skrit, Mott, Vriss, Tallow, Knuck, Pritt, Scabbin, Marn, Ruttle, Kett.

They also accumulate nicknames rapidly. A Ratwretch might introduce himself as: "Mott. Called Three-Doors."

Ask why and he may tell you. Or click twice at his companions, causing everyone except you to laugh.

The Smell of Trouble

Their eyesight is mediocre. Their hearing and smell are extraordinary. More importantly, Ratwretches are intimately sensitive to the physical behavior of the city.

They notice vibration through floors, changes in drafts, water moving through walls, rats fleeing drains, brick dust falling from ceilings and gas where there wasn't gas yesterday.

A Ratwretch may leave a tunnel hours before a collapse because: "Wall tastes wrong."

Engineers dismiss such statements. Experienced sewer workers don't.

Fogport has an old expression: "When the wretches start climbing, find higher ground."

Ratwretches and Ordinary Rats

This is perhaps the strangest thing about them. Ordinary rats are terrified of Ratwretches.

They do not command rats. They do not speak to rats. They don't keep rats as pets. A common brown rat encountering a Ratwretch usually freezes, screams, or runs.

Ratwretches themselves find rats disgusting.

Calling a Ratwretch a rat is therefore not merely insulting. It's approximately equivalent to calling a human an ape while throwing garbage at him. Many tavern fights have begun this way.

Ratwretches and the Feral Children

Ratwretches avoid certain territories claimed by the Feral Children, especially tunnels beneath Nine Spoons. The children know many Ratwretch entrances. The Ratwretches know many of theirs. Neither side considers this information sufficient reason to visit.

Occasionally they trade. Nobody enjoys watching.

Why Fogport Hates Them

Some of the hatred is prejudice. Some of it is fear. And some Ratwretches really are awful.

There are Ratwretch burglars who can enter houses through spaces their owners didn't know existed. Ratwretch gangs strip abandoned buildings of copper overnight. Some warrens demand payment from businesses built over their territory. Cornered Ratwretches are vicious fighters.

And every Fogporter knows somebody who swears they woke at three in the morning and heard: scritch. scritch. scritch. Inside the wall.

But Ratwretches aren't a hive, an evil race or an underground army. They're another population trying to occupy Fogport. They have families, trades, criminals, cowards, bullies, craftsmen, drunks, grandparents and children.

Fogport simply wishes they would do it somewhere else.

Common Ratwretch Aspects

  • There Is Always Another Way In
  • One Shoulder, Sideways, Breath Out
  • Borrowed Doesn't Mean Stolen
  • We Hear the Building Breathing
  • Nobody Wants Us Here

Trouble

Treated Like Vermin

And there is one piece of Nine Spoons advice concerning Ratwretches that Byl has heard since childhood:

Never chase a Ratwretch into a hole.

If the hole is big enough for you to follow him...

he chose that hole.
